landing.beforeAfter.eyebrow.description: Small label above the transformer demo section title

landing.beforeAfter.outro.message: The output panel shows the first of the three documents this fixture produces, verbatim from the committed file. Where source data has genuine gaps — a description, a classification — the CLI can fill them with optional AI enrichment. {docsLink}

landing.beforeAfter.subtitle.message: A vendor's export, a mapping you write once, and the document the CLI produces — a back squat any FDS reader can validate. All three panels are files that ship in this repository, and CI runs this exact transform against the published schema on every change.

landing.beforeAfter.title.message: See it work on a back squat

landing.capabilities.bodyAtlas.purpose.message: Anatomical regions and the bindings that let any illustration draw them.

landing.capabilities.equipment.purpose.message: What a movement needs, and how a machine loads — so a prescription stays reproducible.

landing.capabilities.exercises.purpose.message: A movement described once — classification, muscle targets, equipment, metrics.

landing.capabilities.eyebrow.description: Small label above the capabilities section title

landing.capabilities.layer1.blurb.message: A common vocabulary for the fitness domain. Static, cacheable, mirrorable, diffable. Adopt it alone if all you want is a canonical exercise list every system reads the same way.

landing.capabilities.layer2.blurb.message: How to train, composed from the library. Sets, reps, tempo, load, rest and zones assemble into sessions, and sessions into multi-week plans — one schema each, however the training is structured.

landing.capabilities.muscles.purpose.message: Named anatomy that renderers and taxonomies can bind to without agreeing on artwork.

landing.capabilities.prescription.purpos.message: Load, reps, tempo, rest, RPE/RIR and set schemes — the vocabulary of intensity.

landing.capabilities.programs.purpose.message: A schedule of sessions over weeks — periodisation and progression, by reference not by copy.

landing.capabilities.subtitle.message: FDS defines a shared vocabulary and, on top of it, how to prescribe training with that vocabulary. Either layer can be adopted on its own.

landing.capabilities.workouts.purpose.message: One session. Straight sets, supersets, circuits, EMOM, AMRAP and intervals share a single schema.

landing.noPersonalData.cached.detail.message: A library sits behind a CDN like any other static asset.

landing.noPersonalData.diffed.detail.message: Two versions compare cleanly, because nothing in them is a person.

landing.noPersonalData.eyebrow.description: Small label above the no-personal-data section title

landing.noPersonalData.footnote.message: A document that describes nobody is one you can publish freely. What this deliberately excludes, and why, is on the {roadmapLink}.

landing.noPersonalData.mirrored.detail.message: Anyone can republish a catalog without inheriting an obligation.

landing.noPersonalData.shared.detail.message: No consent, DPA or privacy review gates an exchange.

landing.noPersonalData.subtitle.message: No athlete identity, no bodyweight, no one-rep maxes, no performed or logged results — none of it is in the standard, and none of it ever will be. A prescription that would need a personal number references it instead of carrying it. That constraint is exactly why an FDS document can be:

landing.problem.eyebrow.description: Small label above the problem section title

landing.problem.fragmentation.descriptio.message: Apps cannot interoperate. The same exercise has different IDs, names, and structures everywhere.

landing.problem.lockIn.description.message: Your exercise library, workouts and programs live in one app’s private format. Switch, and you re-enter them by hand or leave them behind.

landing.problem.outro.message: So what does FDS actually define? →

landing.problem.overhead.description.message: Building from scratch or adding integrations? Either way, you're defining exercise models alone. No shared vocabulary to build on.

landing.problem.subtitle.message: The same back squat, four private spellings. None of them can read the others, so every integration is built by hand and every export is a dead end.

landing.problem.title.message: Every platform speaks a different language

landing.quickStart.exampleFooter.message: The published example for the exercise entity — a back squat, verbatim from the spec.
landing.quickStart.exampleFooter.description: Caption under the example document panel in the quick start section

landing.quickStart.eyebrow.description: Small label above the quick start section title

landing.quickStart.step1.description.message: Download the JSON Schema to validate your exercise data.

landing.quickStart.step2.description.message: Structure your exercise data using the FDS format. Start minimal, expand as needed.

landing.quickStart.step3.description.message: Use any JSON Schema validator (ajv, jsonschema, etc.) to ensure compliance.

landing.quickStart.step4.description.message: Use the FDS Transformer CLI to convert your existing data to FDS format with optional AI enrichment.

landing.quickStart.subtitle.message: FDS is JSON Schema at stable URLs. If your stack can read JSON, it can implement the standard — start with the schema and any validator you already use.

landing.solution.ext.namespaces.text.message: Prefix custom fields with {prefix} to add platform-specific data that travels with the standard.

landing.solution.ext.promotion.text.message: An extension several implementers adopt can be proposed into the core schema through the RFC process.

landing.solution.ext.safe.text.message: Other platforms ignore unknown namespaces. Your custom data never breaks their imports.

landing.solution.ext.subtitle.message: Add custom fields without breaking compatibility.

landing.solution.eyebrow.description: Small label above the solution section title

landing.solution.highlight.anyStack.message: Any stack that can read JSON can implement it.

landing.solution.highlight.exchangeForma.message: No forced architecture changes — FDS is an exchange format, not your database schema.

landing.solution.highlight.validates.message: Every document validates against a published JSON Schema.

landing.solution.subtitle.message: One standard replaces point-to-point integrations. Each platform writes one exporter and one importer against FDS, and connects to everyone who did the same.

landing.trust.eyebrow.description: Small label above the stability section title

landing.trust.frozen.description.message: Every published schema is pinned by sha256 and never changes. A new version ships in a new directory beside the old one, which stays served — so a client pinned to an older release keeps resolving.

landing.trust.governance.description.message: Every entity arrived through a public RFC, and changes are additive by rule. The standard is developed in the open so no single vendor can quietly redefine the format under you.

landing.trust.perEntity.description.message: A release names a set of entity versions, not one number they all share. Entities move independently, and the release manifest is generated from the published tree — so what the site says is published is what is published.

landing.trust.stat.entities.message: entity schemas, each frozen at a permanent URL

landing.trust.stat.examples.message: worked examples shipped beside the schemas

landing.trust.stat.scenarios.message: training scenarios, every one with a worked example

landing.trust.subtitle.message: A format you integrate once should not move under you.

whyFds.audience.message: For platform owners, product leads and coaches deciding what format their training content lives in. No schemas on this page — the {useCasesLink} show the same argument with the actual files.

whyFds.close.ghostButton.message: What you can do with it

whyFds.close.primaryButton.message: See it work on a back squat

whyFds.close.text.message: The shortest path to a decision is watching it work: a real vendor export, mapped once, becoming a document any FDS reader validates.

whyFds.eyebrow.description: Small label above the /why-fds page title

whyFds.independence.asideNote.message: Each entity at its own version, every URL frozen. Superseded versions stay served.

whyFds.independence.body1.message: A private format changes when its owner needs it to. FDS is built so that cannot happen to you: every published schema is frozen at a permanent public URL and never edited in place. New versions are additive and ship beside the old ones, which stay served — so a system built against the standard keeps working, on the schedule you choose.

whyFds.independence.body2.message: The standard itself is developed in the open, through public RFCs — no single company can quietly redefine what your documents mean. And adopting it requires no SDK and no proprietary tooling: it is plain JSON with published schemas, validated by tools your team already uses.

whyFds.independence.title.message: Independence: a format no vendor can move under you

whyFds.interoperability.asideLink.message: See it work on a back squat →

whyFds.interoperability.asideNote.message: A real vendor export, one mapping, and the validating output — all three are files in the repository.

whyFds.interoperability.body1.message: Every integration between two fitness systems today starts with the same meeting: what counts as an exercise, whose muscle taxonomy wins, how a superset is written down. The result is a bespoke mapping that breaks whenever either side changes — multiplied by every partner you add.

whyFds.interoperability.body2.message: A shared vocabulary collapses that to one mapping: yours, into the standard, written once. Two systems that both speak FDS line up without ever having met. The {transformerLink} does the mapping for data you already have — the landing page shows it running on a real vendor export.

whyFds.interoperability.title.message: Interoperability: integrate once, not once per partner

whyFds.lede.message: Exercise libraries, equipment catalogs and training programs are assets. Today they are stored in whatever private shape each platform invented, which quietly turns them into liabilities: hard to move, expensive to connect, gone when a vendor is. FDS is an open, vendor-neutral format that makes them documents — portable, connectable and readable on their own.

whyFds.meta.description.message: The business case for the Fitness Data Standard: training content that outlives the app that made it, integrations built once, and a format no vendor can move under you.

whyFds.meta.title.description: Browser tab title of the /why-fds page

whyFds.noPeople.asideNote.message: How a program references a person's numbers without ever carrying them.

whyFds.noPeople.body1.message: FDS describes training content, not the people doing the training. There is no athlete identity, no bodyweight, no logged result anywhere in the standard. A catalog or program in FDS is a document about nobody — it can be published, shared with partners, cached and mirrored without carrying personal-data obligations along with it.

whyFds.noPeople.body2.message: Where a program needs a personal number — a percentage of someone's max, say — it references it rather than carrying it. Performed results are deliberately out of scope until there is a consent and privacy model worthy of them; the {roadmapLink} is explicit about that line.

whyFds.portability.asideNote.message: A complete exercise from a published file — the document that moves.

whyFds.portability.body1.message: Most fitness platforms will give you your data on the way out. What they give you is a file only they understand — every exercise name, muscle list and set structure encoded in their private vocabulary. In practice, migrating means rebuilding your content by hand on the other side.

whyFds.portability.body2.message: In FDS, a catalog or a program is a document in a published format. Any system that reads the standard reads it, with the meaning intact — a back squat arrives as a back squat, with the muscles it targets and the way it is measured. Moving platforms becomes moving files.

whyFds.portability.title.message: Portability: an export that means something

whyFds.title.message: Training content should outlive the software that made it.

whyFds.today.asideNote.message: Every training structure the schemas express, each row backed by an example CI validates.

whyFds.today.body1.message: FDS is new. The schemas, the transformer and the AI knowledge pack are published and ready to build against, and the reference tooling in this repository is their first user. There are no third-party adopters to point to yet, and this site will not invent any — what you see claimed is what the repository can prove.

whyFds.today.body2.message: That timing is the opportunity in disguise: what the first stable release locks in is still open, and {earlyAdoptersLink} are the ones deciding it.
